title: The fastest path to more power | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Interchange Recharged hosts CTC Global's JD Sitton and Theodore Paradise to argue that carbon-core advanced conductors can roughly double capacity on existing rights-of-way in about 18 months, versus five to seven years for a line rebuild and 10 to 15 years for a new parallel line. The framing is that the binding constraint on serving AI and electrification load is build time and permitting, not conductor technology, which already exists and is underused.

insights.claim: AI, data centres, electrification and new industrial load are arriving on the power system faster than utilities can build generation and transmission on conventional project timelines, making the capacity squeeze an operational reality rather than a forecast.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Any grid solution whose payoff depends on a 5-10 year build is effectively out of the money for near-term load; capital rotates toward things deliverable inside two years.
insights.quote: The pressure on the power system is no longer theoretical.
insights.locator: The pressure on the power system is no longer theoretical

insights.claim: The US grid was already strained before AI demand appeared, with aging generation, electrification-driven load growth and mounting congestion testing the system; AI changed the pace of the problem rather than creating it.
insights.speaker: Theodore Paradise, CTC Global
insights.so_what: Reframes data-centre load as an accelerant on a pre-existing structural deficit, which means grid-capex demand persists even if AI build-out slows.
insights.quote: the grid was already under strain before AI accelerated the problem
insights.locator: As Theodore argues, the grid was already under strain

insights.claim: The scarce resource in power delivery is capacity on wires already in the ground and overhead, so squeezing more throughput from existing assets is positioned as the least glamorous but most consequential lever available to utilities.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Points investors at asset-optimisation suppliers (conductors, dynamic line rating, grid-enhancing tech) rather than only at greenfield transmission developers.
insights.locator: One of the least glamorous but potentially most consequential answers

insights.claim: Replacing traditional steel-core conductors with carbon-core alternatives sharply reduces sag, increases thermal performance and in many cases doubles capacity on existing rights-of-way without rebuilding towers.
insights.speaker: JD Sitton and Theodore Paradise, CTC Global
insights.so_what: A doubling of line rating without new towers or land changes the cost curve for incremental delivered MW and competes directly with new-build transmission capex.
insights.locator: replacing traditional steel-core conductors with carbon-core alternatives

insights.claim: A reconductoring project can be completed in roughly 18 months, against five to seven years for a line rebuild and 10 to 15 years for a new parallel transmission line.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: The 18-month versus 10-15-year spread is the core investable number: it is the only transmission-side option that matches data-centre commissioning schedules.
insights.quote: A reconductoring project can be completed in roughly 18 months, compared with five to seven years for a rebuild and 10 to 15 years for a new parallel line.
insights.locator: What changes in this moment is the pace

insights.claim: Because reconductoring reuses existing rights-of-way, the speed advantage compounds into lower cost, less permitting friction and reduced community opposition, rather than being purely a scheduling benefit.
insights.speaker: JD Sitton and Theodore Paradise, CTC Global
insights.so_what: Permitting and siting risk is the main killer of transmission IRRs; solutions that avoid new land acquisition carry structurally lower execution risk.
insights.locator: It is also about cutting costs, easing permitting friction

insights.claim: Advanced conductors improve line safety by lowering heat-driven sag and therefore the risk of vegetation contact, tying grid-capacity upgrades to wildfire-ignition risk reduction.
insights.speaker: JD Sitton and Theodore Paradise, CTC Global
insights.so_what: Creates a second justification path through safety and wildfire-liability budgets, which utilities can fund even when capacity spend is contested.
insights.locator: improving safety by lowering the risk of heat-driven sag and vegetation contact

insights.claim: Reconductoring is framed as making better use of capital already committed to the system, meaning incremental capacity is bought without a proportional increase in rate base exposure.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Cuts against the regulated-utility incentive to maximise rate base, so adoption may lag economics where returns are earned on new capex.
insights.locator: make better use of capital already committed to the system

themes.theme: What reliability means in the new load era

insights.claim: Reliability itself needs redefining for a grid characterised by bigger load swings, tighter operating margins and rising public scrutiny over cost, not just by traditional outage metrics.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Regulatory definitions of reliability drive what utilities are allowed to spend on; a redefinition reshapes which vendors get funded.
insights.locator: the episode asks what reliability should mean in a grid era

insights.claim: Real-time line monitoring paired with higher-rated conductors lets operators run lines with greater confidence under stressed conditions, converting static safety margins into usable capacity.
insights.speaker: JD Sitton and Theodore Paradise, CTC Global
insights.so_what: Monitoring plus advanced conductors is a stacked play; watch for utilities pairing the two in rate filings as a cheaper alternative to new lines.
insights.locator: From wildfire resilience to real-time line monitoring

insights.claim: Advanced conductors are explicitly not presented as a silver bullet but as a proven and underused tool, an unusually hedged framing for a sponsored technology discussion.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Signals the bottleneck is utility adoption behaviour and regulation rather than technology maturity, so track procurement decisions, not product announcements.
insights.quote: advanced conductors are presented not as a silver bullet, but as a proven, underused tool that could help utilities move faster
insights.locator: advanced conductors are presented not as a silver bullet

insights.claim: The implied indictment of the industry is that one of the simplest grid-capacity solutions may have been available all along while utilities pursued slower, costlier new-build paths.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: If regulators reach the same conclusion, expect prudency pressure on utilities that chose new lines over reconductoring, and faster mandated adoption.
insights.quote: whether the industry will look back on this moment and conclude that one of the simplest grid-capacity solutions was available all along
insights.locator: The larger question running through the episode

themes.theme: CTC Global's installed base and positioning

insights.claim: CTC Global claims the position of world's leading manufacturer of high-capacity advanced conductors, with ACCC conductors deployed over more than two decades and more than 300 utility and industrial customers across 69 countries and 30 US states.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: An installed base spanning 69 countries means the technology risk is already retired; the open question is US utility procurement pace, not qualification.
insights.quote: trusted by more than 300 utilities and industrial customers across 69 countries and 30 US states
insights.locator: CTC Global is accelerating access to energy

insights.claim: CTC Global's sales pitch is framed as adding the greatest amount of electricity at the lowest capital cost, positioning advanced conductors on a dollars-per-incremental-MW basis rather than on a product-performance basis.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cost-per-delivered-MW is the metric utilities and regulators will benchmark against gas peakers, storage and new lines; that comparison drives the addressable market.
insights.quote: add the greatest amount of electricity at the lowest capital cost
